subtopics.title: Solids, polyhedra and terms
subtopics.theory_md:
A **polyhedron** is a solid bounded by plane faces. **Prism**: two equal parallel bases joined by rectangular faces. **Pyramid**: one base, triangular faces meeting at the **apex**. **Solids of revolution**: cylinder, cone (generators join apex to the base circle), sphere. **Regular polyhedra** (equal regular faces): tetrahedron 4, cube 6, octahedron 8, dodecahedron 12, icosahedron 20 faces; Euler $F+V=E+2$.

The **axis** joins the centres of the two ends (base centre to apex for a pyramid). The **slant edge** runs from the apex to a base corner. A **right** solid has its axis perpendicular to the base.
subtopics.basics_md: Every solid here is fixed by two numbers: the size of its base (side of a regular polygon, or diameter of a circle) and the length of its axis. Prisms and cylinders keep the same base at both ends; pyramids and cones come to a point.
key_points: Prism: two equal parallel bases; pyramid: one base plus an apex
Cylinder and cone are solids of revolution
Axis joins base centre to the opposite end or apex; slant edge joins apex to a corner
Regular polyhedra: 4, 6, 8, 12, 20 faces; F + V = E + 2

subtopics.title: Solid in simple positions
subtopics.theory_md:
In the **simple position** the axis is perpendicular to one reference plane, and the base is parallel to it.

- **Axis perpendicular to HP** (base on HP): top view (TV) is the **true shape of the base**; front view (FV) is a rectangle (prism, cylinder) or triangle (pyramid, cone) of height = axis length.
- **Axis perpendicular to VP**: FV is the true base; TV is the rectangle or triangle.
- **Axis parallel to both planes**: both views are rectangles (prism) or triangles (pyramid).

Resting on a **rectangular face** (prism) means the axis is parallel to HP and a base edge is perpendicular to the plane of the views. Draw the view that shows the true shape first, then project the other.
subtopics.basics_md: When a face is parallel to a plane, its view on that plane is its true shape. Make the base parallel to the plane you are looking at, draw the true shape, then project the second view by drawing projector lines and measuring the axis length.
key_points: Axis perpendicular to HP: TV is the true base, FV height = axis length
Axis perpendicular to VP: FV is the true base, TV is rectangle or triangle
Draw the view with the true shape first, then project
Hidden edges dashed, corners labelled

**Front view:** draw $XY$. Project the six corners down to $XY$ to get the 60 mm base line (and the nearer corners). Mark the apex $o'$ 60 mm above the base centre. Join $o'$ to the base points.
**Visibility:** all edges seen from the front are drawn solid; the rear corner edges coincide in FV. Label corners $a, b, \ldots, f$ and apex $o$.
**Result:** TV a hexagon with lines to the centre; FV a triangle 60 mm base by 60 mm high.

subtopics.title: Changing position: the stage rule
subtopics.theory_md:
Every inclined position is built from the simple position in **stages**; the same views are only redrawn, never changed in shape.

- **Inclination to HP**: the FV is tilted (rotated about the resting point or edge). **The TV is then projected**, with horizontal distances taken from the previous TV and projectors from the new FV.
- **Inclination to VP**: the TV is rotated (its shape does not change). **The FV is then projected**, keeping **heights** from the previous FV.
- **Rule:** while a tilt or turn is made, the other view's measures (heights or plan lengths) stay constant.

Order: first the condition that fixes the axis to HP, then the one to VP (for HP-based solids). True inclinations to a plane appear true only in the view on the plane parallel to the line.
subtopics.basics_md: Imagine the solid lying flat on the table, then lifting one end (tilt: the front view changes) and then turning the whole thing about a vertical line (turn: the top view just rotates). A rotation keeps the height of every point the same, so the front view heights carry over.
key_points: Tilt to HP: redraw the FV tilted, then project the TV
Turn to VP: rotate the TV, then project the FV
Heights stay fixed during a turn, plan distances stay fixed during a tilt
Each view in a stage is the same shape as in the previous stage until projected anew

questions.q: State the rule for drawing a solid with its axis inclined to the HP and its plan of axis inclined to the VP. Why can it not be done in one step?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Rule (three stages):**
1. **Stage I:** draw the solid in the simple position (base parallel to HP), TV and FV.
2. **Stage II:** redraw the FV with the axis tilted to the given angle with $XY$ (resting point or edge kept on $XY$); project the TV.
3. **Stage III:** rotate the Stage II TV so the plan of the axis (or the resting edge) makes the given angle with $XY$; project the final FV with heights from Stage II.
It cannot be done in one step because both inclinations are measured in different planes; the second is measured on the TV which exists only after the first tilt.
points: Stage I simple position
Stage II tilt FV, project TV
Stage III rotate TV, project FV with heights from Stage II
Second angle can only be set on the TV after the first tilt

subtopics.title: Prism resting on an edge: axis to HP, edge to VP
subtopics.theory_md:
Data: base edge on HP, axis at $\theta$ to HP, the resting edge at $\varphi$ to VP.

1. **Stage I:** TV = true base with the resting edge **perpendicular to $XY$** (a point in the FV if axis is vertical). FV = rectangle (height = axis).
2. **Stage II:** redraw the FV with the axis at $\theta$ to $XY$, resting edge (a point) on $XY$. Project TV: axis length in TV $=L\cos\theta$, height of the far end $=L\sin\theta$.
3. **Stage III:** rotate the TV so the **resting edge** makes $\varphi$ with $XY$. Project FV, heights from Stage II.

Example: axis 100 mm, $\theta=45^\circ$: height $=100\sin45^\circ=70.71$ mm, TV length $=70.71$ mm. If the *edge* is given as inclined to the HP instead, the data are contradictory; read it as inclined to the VP.
subtopics.basics_md: To rest a prism on an edge, picture it standing on its base, then lean it over the base edge like a falling box. Leaning (tilt) is the HP angle; then you turn the box on the floor (turn) for the VP angle.
key_points: Stage I: resting edge perpendicular to XY in the TV
Stage II: tilt the FV so axis is at theta; heights L sin(theta), plan length L cos(theta)
Stage III: rotate TV so the resting edge makes phi with XY
Project FV with Stage II heights; dashed hidden lines

questions.q: A square prism, base side 40 mm and axis 80 mm, rests on a base edge on HP. The axis is inclined at 30 degrees to HP and the resting edge is at 60 degrees to VP. Describe the construction of the projections.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Given:** square prism, side 40 mm, axis 80 mm; base edge on HP; axis $30^\circ$ to HP; edge $60^\circ$ to VP.
**Stage I:** TV: a square $abcd$ of side 40 mm with edge $ab$ perpendicular to $XY$, so in the FV $a'b'$ is a point. FV: rectangle $40\times80$ on $XY$.

**Finish:** join corners, dash hidden edges, label all corners.

subtopics.title: Pyramid resting on an edge: axis to HP, edge to VP
subtopics.theory_md:
Same three stages as the prism, with the pyramid's apex.

1. **Stage I:** TV = true base with the resting edge perpendicular to $XY$ and the apex at the centre joined to every corner. FV = triangle on $XY$ with apex at axis height.
2. **Stage II:** tilt the FV so the **axis** makes $\theta$ with $XY$ and the base edge rests on $XY$ (the edge is a point on $XY$). The apex height $=L\sin\theta$ plus the base-centre height. Project TV.
3. **Stage III:** rotate the TV so the resting edge makes $\varphi$ with $XY$, project FV with Stage II heights.

For a regular polygon, the circumradius is $R=\dfrac{s}{2\sin(180^\circ/n)}$ and the inradius (centre to side) is $r=\dfrac{s}{2\tan(180^\circ/n)}$. Pentagon, $s=20$: $R=17.01$ mm, $r=13.76$ mm.
subtopics.basics_md: A pyramid leaning on a base edge: first draw it standing on its base, then tilt it over the edge until the axis is at the given angle, then turn it on the table to the required direction.
key_points: Stage I: base edge perpendicular to XY in the TV, apex at base centre
Stage II: tilt FV so the axis is theta to XY, edge on XY
Stage III: rotate TV so the edge is phi to XY; project FV with Stage II heights
Circumradius R = s / (2 sin(180/n)), inradius r = s / (2 tan(180/n))

subtopics.title: Axis to HP and its plan to VP
subtopics.theory_md:
Data: a corner or edge on HP, **axis at $\theta$ to HP**, **plan (top view) of the axis at $\varphi$ to the VP**.

- In **Stage III** you rotate the TV so the line representing the **axis in the TV** (from the base centre to the apex, or along the prism's axis) makes $\varphi$ with $XY$. This differs from the "edge at $\varphi$" problems, where the resting edge is rotated.
- Stage I: TV with the resting edge perpendicular to $XY$ (an edge) or the resting corner at the correct place (a corner); Stage II: tilt FV to $\theta$; project TV.
- **True angle to VP**: $\sin\psi=\cos\theta\,\sin\varphi$. For $\theta=30^\circ$, $\varphi=45^\circ$: $\sin\psi=0.612$, $\psi=37.76^\circ$.
subtopics.basics_md: 'Plan of the axis' just means the shadow of the axis on the ground. Once the solid is tilted, the shadow of the axis is a line in the top view; you turn the top view until that shadow line makes the given angle with the XY line.

Resting edge or corner is on HP in Stage II
True angle to VP: sin(psi) = cos(theta) sin(phi)
Heights come from Stage II

subtopics.title: Slant edge on HP, and resting on a corner
subtopics.theory_md:
When a pyramid rests on a **slant edge** or a **corner**, Stage II is set by the slant geometry.

- **Slant edge length:** $l=\sqrt{h^2+R^2}$ with $R$ the circumradius. Hexagon, $s=30$ ($R=30$), $h=60$: $l=67.08$ mm.
- **Slant edge on HP** (hexagonal pyramid): tilt the Stage I FV about the base corner until the **slant edge $o'a'$ lies on $XY$**. The axis then makes $\tan^{-1}(R/h)=\tan^{-1}(30/60)=26.57^\circ$ with HP. Stage III: rotate TV so the TV of the slant edge makes the given angle with $XY$.
- **Prism on a corner:** the long edge through the corner (parallel to the axis) is inclined at $\theta$; the opposite base side is turned to $\varphi$ in Stage III; "vertex towards VP" fixes the TV orientation.
- "Base visible" means the base shows in the TV (apex on the far side).
subtopics.basics_md: A pyramid resting on a slant edge lies on one of its sloping edges like a tent lying on one pole. Make that pole lie flat on the ground line and everything else follows from the standard stages.
key_points: Slant edge l = sqrt(h squared + R squared)
Slant edge on HP: tilt FV until o'a' lies on XY; axis angle = tan inverse (R/h)
Stage III: rotate TV so the stated edge makes phi with XY
Corner on HP: long edge at theta; vertex towards VP sets the orientation

topics.topic: Solids of revolution in different positions

subtopics.title: Cylinder and cone: resting on a generator
subtopics.theory_md:
A cylinder or cone is fixed by base diameter $d$ and axis $h$. The cone's **generator** (slant length) is $L=\sqrt{h^2+(d/2)^2}$ and the **semi-apex angle** $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\big(\tfrac{d/2}{h}\big)$.

- **Cone on a generator on HP, axis parallel to VP:** the axis makes angle $\alpha$ with HP (the generator lies on $XY$ in the FV). Stage I: TV circle (12 equal parts), FV triangle. Stage II: tilt the FV about the base point so the generator $o'a'$ lies on $XY$; project TV. The TV is an ellipse (base) with tangents to the apex.
- **Cylinder** on a generator (line) on HP: the axis is parallel to HP; both views rectangles, TV circle if axis perpendicular to VP.

Example: $d=50$, $h=65$: $L=69.64$ mm, $\alpha=21.04^\circ$.
subtopics.basics_md: A cone lying on its side rests on one straight line (generator) touching the floor. Tilting the cone about its base edge until that line is flat on the ground lets you find the angle between the axis and the floor: it equals the half angle at the apex.
key_points: Generator L = sqrt(h squared + r squared); semi-apex angle alpha = tan inverse (r/h)
Cone on a generator: FV generator lies on XY, axis at alpha to HP

subtopics.title: Generator in the VP
subtopics.theory_md:
**A generator in the VP** inclined at $\theta$ to HP with the apex above HP: that generator appears **true length on the FV** and lies on $XY$ in the TV (it is in the VP, so its TV is on the line $XY$).

- Axis inclination to HP $=\theta+\alpha$ (for the usual apex-up case), where $\alpha=\tan^{-1}(r/h)$.
- Stage I: TV circle, FV triangle. Stage II: tilt the FV so the **left (or right) generator makes $\theta$ with $XY$** (the axis therefore makes $\theta+\alpha$). Project TV: the generator's TV lies along $XY$ at the VP.

Example: $d=50$, $h=60$: $L=65$ mm, $\alpha=22.62^\circ$; $\theta=30^\circ$ gives axis at $52.62^\circ$.
subtopics.basics_md: Standing a cone on its side and tilting it so one straight edge of the cone lies against the back wall (the VP). Because the wall is parallel to the front view, that edge shows its real length and its real angle to the floor there.
key_points: Generator in VP is true length in FV and lies on XY in the TV
Axis inclination to HP = theta + alpha (apex up)
Tilt FV so that generator makes theta with XY
Project TV; base circle becomes an ellipse

subtopics.title: Resting on a point of the base circle
subtopics.theory_md:
When the solid rests on **one point of the base circle** (point touching HP or VP), the axis is inclined to the reference plane and then turned.

- **Axis at $\theta$ to HP and $\varphi$ to VP** (HP-based): Stage I: TV circle, FV on $XY$. Stage II: tilt the FV so the axis makes $\theta$ with $XY$ and a base point is on $XY$; project TV. Stage III: rotate TV so the axis makes $\varphi$ with $XY$; project FV (Stage II heights).
- **Resting point on the VP** (VP-based): do the same with the planes swapped: axis perpendicular to VP in Stage I (FV a circle); tilt the **TV**; then rotate the **FV**.
- **Relation:** if the axis is at $\theta$ to HP and its plan at $\varphi$ to VP, the true angle to VP is $\sin\psi=\cos\theta\sin\varphi$.
subtopics.basics_md: A cone or cylinder resting on one point of its rim is like a coin tilted on its edge. Tilt it for the first angle, then turn it about the vertical for the second.
key_points: HP-based: tilt FV for theta, rotate TV for phi
VP-based: tilt TV for the VP angle, rotate FV for the HP-plane angle
Base circle becomes an ellipse in the inclined views

questions.q: A cone of axis 50 mm rests on a point of its base circle with the axis at 30 degrees to HP. Find the rise of the apex above the base centre and the plan length of the axis.
questions.model_answer_md:
Rise of apex above the base centre $=h\sin30^\circ=50\times0.5=\mathbf{25\ mm}$.
Plan length of axis $=h\cos30^\circ=\mathbf{43.30\ mm}$.
Stage III turns the TV only, so heights stay as in Stage II.
points: Rise = h sin(theta) = 25 mm
Plan length = h cos(theta) = 43.30 mm
Heights unchanged in Stage III

questions.q: A cylinder of axis 65 mm is inclined at 45 degrees to the VP and the front view of the axis is at 45 degrees to XY. Find its true inclination to HP.
questions.model_answer_md:
Plan or front view length of axis in Stage II: $65\cos45^\circ=45.96$ mm.
Height component: $45.96\sin45^\circ=32.5$ mm.
$\sin\theta=32.5/65=0.5$, so $\theta=\mathbf{30^\circ}$ to HP.
points: FV length 65 cos45 = 45.96 mm
Height 32.5 mm
True angle to HP 30 degrees
